transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-07-14 16:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (BrightApps CTO), Maya Chen (Platform Eng), Arjun Patel (Infra)

Summary: quick recap of last week's run, results from canary traffic, focus today is autoscale sizing and burst planning for Dedicated pool.

00:00 Jordan: ok everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off, quick agenda: sizing review, autoscale options, burst windows, and action items. Priya is going to run the bench details then we'll go to q's.
00:18 Liam: great, quick note first, we did see those latency spikes in the 99th on Tuesday when syncs hit, it looked like the KV cache was cold, or maybe the K V cache — the prefix caching didn't kick in.
00:35 Priya: yeah we saw that, our canary run shows cold-starts for long seq requests, the KV cache warmup time is about 30s under the current setup. We're thinking about a small pre-warm strategy.
01:02 Maya: our typical user sessions generate a mix: 60% short prompts (<256 tokens), 30% mid (256-2k), 10% long (2k-20k). But during batch imports we get heavy long requests that cause the spikes.
01:20 Jordan: that's helpful — we'll need the full seq-length distribution file, that helps pick the model variant and kernel selection. For Dedicated sizing we care about sustained throughput and burst headroom.
01:45 Priya: two levers for autoscale: scheduled (time-of-day scaling) and reactive (queue depth/cpu utilization). For Redwood Dedicated we also support a burst pool: reserved baseline plus burst capacity that can kick in for short windows.
02:12 Arjun: how does burst billing work? if we go over the baseline, is billing per-second? we need to map to our cost model.
02:25 Jordan: burst is metered; you'll pay higher unit cost for burst vms/gpus but it's only for the duration of burst usage. We'll email a sample cost calc (Jordan).
02:40 Priya: technical detail — when a burst node comes up there's a model load time and kv cache cold penalty; we mitigate by pre-loading a lightweight model artifact and using prefix caching to reduce per-token overhead. There's also an option to keep a small set of warm workers ready.
03:05 Liam: what's the warm workers tradeoff vs cost? we don't want to over-provision baseline.
03:18 Priya: right — small warm pool reduces 99th latency but increases baseline cost. Example: for your 95th SLO of 400ms, with warm pool of 2 workers we hit SLO at 200 rps, otherwise we'd need larger baseline. We'll show numbers in the sizing sheet.
03:45 Maya: also concerned about cold KV eviction when big long requests evict entries used by short interactive requests — any config to prioritize small seq cache?
04:00 Priya: yes there's cache policies; we can configure TTL and LRU weights. Redwood Dedicated supports prioritized KV namespaces for interactive traffic. We'll propose settings.
04:25 Alex: note for compliance — BrightApps asked about audit logs and KMS; Jordan will share security docs.
04:40 Jordan: yes, security pack will be attached, includes KMS integrations, audit log retention and SSO/SAML notes.
05:02 Arjun: back to autoscale policies — what triggers reactive scale? queue length, percent GPU util, or latency threshold?
05:15 Priya: multiple options. Common: queue depth + pending request age; we also have an adaptive policy that watches 95/99 latency and scales preemptively. For Dedicated we let you set min baseline, max capacity, and burst margin.
05:45 Liam: can we set scheduled rules plus reactive override? like scheduled baseline at 9-5, but reactive >some threshold spins up extra nodes.
05:58 Priya: absolutely, that's the recommended pattern: scheduled baseline for predictable work plus reactive scaling for unexpected bursts. You can set cooldown windows and max burst minutes per day to control cost.
06:20 Maya: what's the typical spin-up time for a burst worker? if it's 60-90s that's problematic for sudden spikes.
06:32 Priya: cold spin-up for a new GPU worker is ~45-90s depending on model size and cloud region; with model warmers and preloading we can reduce effective tail to ~15-30s for many cases. For very latency-sensitive flows we recommend keeping a small warm standby.
07:00 Arjun: can the warm standby share KV cache across workers or is it per-worker?
07:12 Priya: KV cache is per-model-serving group but we also have a shared prefix cache layer — it's not a single central DB, it's more of a coordinated cache, so warming one worker helps but not full coverage. We'll detail in doc.
07:40 Liam: we ran a short stress test last week with mixed batch sizes and saw token throughput drop after sustained 10 minutes, likely due to slot contention on the GPU. Could be batch scheduling. Any mitigations?
07:58 Priya: continuous batching in the runtime is meant to help, but you can tweak batching window and max batch size. Also choose quantized model variants (8-bit) to increase capacity at slightly lower quality. Redwood Optimize gave a recommendation for your profile last week.
08:22 Maya: yes we looked at Redwood Optimize notes, it suggested q4_8bit variant for the long generation jobs. But we need to validate quality.
08:40 Priya: agreed, so plan: benchmark both fp16 and 8-bit variants with your sample prompts. Priya will run these.
09:05 Jordan: on pricing, dedicated tiers show baseline cost per GPU plus burst premium; I'll send a sample calc with your traffic histogram to show 3 scenarios: conservative baseline, scheduled + reactive, and small baseline + big burst.
09:30 Liam: timeline — we want to decide sizing for pilot by end of month. Doable?
09:37 Alex: yes that's the target; we want the bench results and histograms this week so Redwood can propose final sizing.
09:50 Priya: technical note: when burst nodes are provisioned they may load a slightly different kernel selection; that can cause minor output differences — usually negligible but flagging for QA.
10:10 Arjun: any limits on concurrent streams per GPU we should know?
10:20 Priya: it's model dependent, but we can present expected concurrency for your model family. For example with the current model, one GPU can handle ~80 concurrent short-streams or ~8 long generation streams given your seq mix. We'll put exact numbers in the sizing sheet.
11:00 Maya: can we get a sample autoscale policy? we'd like to see threshold examples and cooldown values.
11:12 Jordan: yes, Jordan will draft 2-3 policy templates: low-cost, balanced, low-latency.
11:25 Liam: also want to understand failure modes; if burst hits max, what's graceful degradation?
11:34 Priya: two options — queue with backpressure (delays) or fallback to a cheaper model (lower quality). We support automatic fallback routes; you can choose a lower-cost model variant or an offline cached response for non-critical requests.
11:55 Arjun: any network/VPC specifics for Dedicated? peering latency could matter for your on-prem calls.
12:08 Priya: Dedicated can be deployed in VPC with private peering; egress is configurable. For on-prem we'll need to do a deep dive on network topology, we'll schedule that.
12:30 Jordan: ok let's recap next steps — Priya runs throughput bench and model variant comparisons; Arjun shares histograms and burst windows; Jordan shares pricing and autoscale templates; Maya confirms compliance question list. We'll aim to reconvene after bench results.
12:58 Liam: thanks all, that covers it.
13:05 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll stop recording.

Notes: transcript contains typical auto-transcribe artifacts — occasional speaker mislabels and punctuation issues. References: sizing spreadsheet (link: /redwood/shared/pilot-sizing-BrightApps.xlsx), security pack (link: /redwood/security/brightapps-secext.pdf)
